concepts.name: Origins and Establishment of the Indo-Greek Kingdom
key_dimensions: Breakaway from the Seleucid Empire and the role of Diodotus I in founding Bactrian Greeks
Distinction between Bactrian Greeks (Central Asia) and Indo-Greeks (Indian subcontinent) — a common UPSC trap
Role of Demetrius I in crossing the Hindu Kush and establishing Indo-Greek presence in India
Geographic extent: regions of modern Afghanistan, Pakistan, and northwestern India

concepts.name: Menander I (Milinda) — The Most Celebrated Indo-Greek Ruler
key_dimensions: Identification as the greatest Indo-Greek king and his extensive territorial conquests reaching the Gangetic plain
Conversion to Buddhism and the Milindapanha (Questions of Milinda) — a Pali Buddhist text recording his dialogue with Nagasena
Milindapanha as a literary-philosophical source vs. numismatic evidence — cross-referencing source types
His posthumous treatment: relics divided among cities (similar to Buddhist tradition for monks), suggesting deep Buddhist reverence

concepts.name: Milindapanha: Content, Significance, and Source Value
key_dimensions: Structure: Philosophical dialogue between King Milinda and Buddhist monk Nagasena on Buddhist doctrines
Its inclusion in Theravada Buddhist canon in Southeast Asia — significance for religious history
Use as a historical source: corroborating Menander's rule, capital Sagala (modern Sialkot), and Buddhist patronage
UPSC trap: Milindapanha is a Pali text, not Sanskrit; written in a question-answer format, not a chronicle

concepts.name: Numismatic Evidence as the Primary Source for Indo-Greek History
key_dimensions: Why coins are the principal source: absence of literary records from within the kingdom
Bilingual coins (Greek on obverse, Kharosthi/Brahmi on reverse) as evidence of cultural synthesis
Introduction of the practice of portraiture on coins — a Greek innovation that influenced subsequent Indian coinage
Information derivable from coins: ruler's name, title, religion, chronology, and territorial extent

concepts.name: Bilingual and Bilingual-Biscript Coinage of Indo-Greeks
key_dimensions: Use of Greek language alongside Prakrit (in Kharosthi script) — first use of Kharosthi on coins
Significance for decipherment of Kharosthi script and cross-referencing with Greek
Distinction: bilingual (two languages) vs. biscript — UPSC often conflates these
Legacy: inspired later Kushana and Shaka rulers to adopt similar bilingual coin practices

concepts.name: Indo-Greek Contributions to Indian Coinage and Art
key_dimensions: Introduction of the die-struck coin technique replacing the earlier punch-marked coin tradition
Portraiture on coins: realistic profile images of rulers — a Hellenistic tradition new to India
Use of Greek motifs (Zeus, Athena, Hercules) alongside Indian symbols (elephant, bull, dharma wheel)
Influence on Gandhara art: precursor to the blending of Hellenistic and Buddhist artistic traditions

concepts.name: Gandhara Art and the Indo-Greek Cultural Legacy
key_dimensions: Indo-Greek rule as the foundational catalyst for the Gandhara school of art (though Gandhara art flourished under Kushanas)
Key feature: anthropomorphic representation of the Buddha — the first human depiction of Buddha in Indian art
Greek artistic elements: wavy hair, toga-like robes, realistic facial features in Buddhist sculpture
UPSC trap: Gandhara art peaked under Kushanas, not Indo-Greeks — but Indo-Greeks created the precondition

concepts.name: Heliodorus Pillar and Indo-Greek Adoption of Indian Religions
key_dimensions: Heliodorus was a Greek ambassador of Indo-Greek king Antialcidas sent to the court of Shunga king Bhagabhadra
He erected the Garuda pillar at Vidisha (Besnagar) dedicating it to Vasudeva (Vishnu) — earliest known foreign convert to Vaishnavism
Inscription evidence: the pillar inscription is a key epigraphic source for Indo-Greek diplomatic relations with Shungas
Significance: evidence of Indo-Greeks integrating into Indian religious life beyond Buddhism — counters the sole-Buddhism narrative

concepts.name: Political Fragmentation and the Multiplicity of Indo-Greek Kings
key_dimensions: Over 30 Indo-Greek kings are known — most known only from coins, with overlapping reigns suggesting parallel kingdoms
Division into western and eastern Indo-Greek kingdoms after Menander's death
Difficulty in establishing a definitive chronology — UPSC often tests awareness of this historiographical limitation
Contrast with Mauryan centralized empire: Indo-Greek polity was fragmented and feudal in nature

concepts.name: Relationship Between Indo-Greeks and the Shunga Dynasty
key_dimensions: Pushyamitra Shunga's conflict with Indo-Greeks: Patanjali's Mahabhashya mentions 'Yavanas besieged Saketa and Madhyamika'
Debate: Was the Indo-Greek advance into the Gangetic plain successful or repulsed by Shungas?
Heliodorus Pillar as evidence of peaceful diplomatic relations coexisting with military rivalry
UPSC trap: Yavana in Indian texts refers to Greeks (and later generically to foreigners) — not all Yavana references mean Indo-Greeks specifically

concepts.name: The Term 'Yavana' in Indian Literary Tradition
key_dimensions: Etymology: derived from 'Ionia' (Greek region) — Yavana originally meant Ionians/Greeks
Evolution of usage: later applied broadly to all western foreigners (Scythians, Parthians, Arabs)
Sources using Yavana: Arthashastra, Mahabhashya, Manusmriti, Puranas, Milindapanha
UPSC trap: In post-2nd century BCE texts, 'Yavana' may not exclusively mean Greeks — context is critical

concepts.name: Indo-Greek Diplomatic and Trade Relations with Indian Kingdoms
key_dimensions: Heliodorus as ambassador: evidence of formal diplomatic exchange between Indo-Greeks and Shungas
Control of trade routes: Indo-Greeks dominated the northwestern routes connecting India to Central Asia and Mediterranean
Role in facilitating early Silk Route trade — their territory bridged Indian and Hellenistic commercial worlds
Taxila (Takshasila) as a major urban and trade center under Indo-Greek influence

concepts.name: Taxila (Takshasila) Under Indo-Greek Rule
key_dimensions: Taxila as the principal capital and cultural center of Indo-Greek power
Archaeological evidence from Taxila (Sir John Marshall's excavations) showing Hellenistic urban planning
Taxila as a meeting point of Greek, Indian, Persian, and Central Asian cultures
UPSC trap: Taxila was important before Indo-Greeks (Achaemenid, Mauryan periods) — Indo-Greek contribution must be distinguished

concepts.name: Decline of Indo-Greek Power: Causes and Successors
key_dimensions: Internal fragmentation: constant civil wars and division of territory among claimants weakened the state
External pressure: Shaka (Scythian) invasions from the northwest gradually displaced Indo-Greek rulers
The last Indo-Greek ruler: Strato II (c. 10 CE) — overthrown by Indo-Scythians
Sequence of succession: Indo-Greeks → Indo-Scythians (Shakas) → Indo-Parthians → Kushanas — a frequently tested chronological order

concepts.name: Indo-Greek Contributions to Astronomy and the Calendar
key_dimensions: Transmission of Hellenistic astronomical knowledge to India — Yavanajataka (Greek astrology text translated into Sanskrit)
Greek influence on Indian astronomical terminology and zodiac system
Debate on the extent of Greek vs. indigenous Indian astronomical tradition — historiographical dimension
UPSC relevance: often appears in science and technology in ancient India questions

concepts.name: Greek Influence on Indian Dramatic and Theatrical Traditions
key_dimensions: Theory of Greek influence on Sanskrit drama: use of curtain (yavanika — 'Greek curtain'), prologue, dramatic structure
The word 'Yavanika' (curtain in Sanskrit theater) as linguistic evidence of Greek theatrical influence
Debate: indigenous origins of Sanskrit drama vs. Greek influence — not settled conclusively
UPSC trap: This is a contested theory — answers should present it as a hypothesis, not established fact

concepts.name: Religious Policy of Indo-Greek Rulers: Syncretism and Patronage
key_dimensions: Patronage of Buddhism (Menander/Milinda) alongside retention of Greek religious imagery on coins
Adoption of Vaishnavism by Heliodorus — evidence of individual Indo-Greeks embracing different Indian sects
Coins depicting both Greek deities and Indian symbols (elephant, Lakshmi, dharma wheel) — evidence of official syncretism
Contrast with later Kushana policy of religious syncretism — Indo-Greeks as early precedent

concepts.name: Apollodotus I and Demetrius: Early Indo-Greek Expansion into India
key_dimensions: Demetrius I: credited with the initial invasion of India (c. 180 BCE), possibly coinciding with Shunga overthrow of Mauryas
Apollodotus I: first Indo-Greek ruler to reign exclusively in India (not also in Bactria) — marks true 'Indo-Greek' phase
Coins of Apollodotus I found in Sindh and Punjab — evidence of territorial extent
UPSC trap: Demetrius is sometimes confused with Seleucid Demetrius — must specify 'Indo-Greek Demetrius' or 'Demetrius of Bactria'

concepts.name: Sources for Indo-Greek History: A Comparative Assessment
key_dimensions: Primary sources: coins (most reliable), Milindapanha (Pali), Heliodorus Pillar inscription (epigraphic), Patanjali's Mahabhashya
Foreign sources: Strabo, Justin, and other Greek/Roman authors — provide external perspective but with limitations
Absence of a dynastic chronicle or inscription series (unlike Ashokan edicts) — why chronology remains uncertain
UPSC angle: questions on 'which source tells us about X' — e.g., Milindapanha for Menander, coins for most other kings

concepts.name: Indo-Greeks and the Spread of Buddhism to the West
key_dimensions: Menander's conversion as a high-profile example of Buddhism attracting foreign rulers
Indo-Greek territories as a conduit for Buddhist transmission toward Central Asia and eventually China (Silk Route)
Buddhist monasteries and stupas in the Gandhara region receiving Indo-Greek patronage
UPSC trap: The major westward spread of Buddhism occurred more significantly under Kushanas — Indo-Greeks were an earlier, smaller-scale facilitator
